name: amass
purpose: OWASP attack surface mapping and external asset discovery: expands a root domain, ASN, CIDR or address range into a stored graph of subdomains, IP addresses, netblocks, ASNs and organisations, using passive OSINT sources, certificate transparency, zone-transfer attempts, DNS brute force and name alterations
author: Jeff Foley (caffix)
org: OWASP Foundation (Flagship project); owasp-amass GitHub organisation
why_notable: Subdomain enumeration began with DNS zone transfers (AXFR, RFC 1034/1035, later RFC 5936), then wordlist brute force (dnsmap, fierce, dnsenum, dnsrecon), search-engine scraping (theHarvester, Sublist3r), passive DNS (2005) and Certificate Transparency logs (RFC 6962, 2013; crt.sh). In 2017 Jeff Foley, a penetration-testing and red-team lead at National Grid with a background in offensive cyber R&D at Northrop Grumman, built Amass to automate the slow, error-prone recon he did when showing organisations what they look like from the internet. Written in Go, it combined dozens of passive data sources, AXFR, certificate grabs, brute force, name alterations and recursion into one concurrent engine. More importantly, it stored how each name links to IPs, netblocks, ASNs and organisations, which turned enumeration into attack surface mapping. It became an OWASP project in 2018 and later an OWASP Flagship project. The Open Asset Model (OAM), announced at DEF CON 30 (2022), and the asset-db library (SQLite or PostgreSQL) arrived with v4 in 2023. v4.2 removed the db subcommand, and v5 (2025) split collection into a background engine with a REST API on 127.0.0.1:4000. In v5 the CLI is enum (collect) plus subs, track, viz and assoc (query the graph); the old intel subcommand and enum -o/-json are gone. As of November 2026 it is at v5.1.3 under Apache-2.0. Pentesters and red teams use it to build the target list before scanning, bug bounty hunters run it nightly and diff with amass track to catch new hosts first, ASM and blue teams schedule it against a shared Postgres asset-db to find shadow IT and dangling CNAMEs, OSINT and threat-intel analysts pivot through ASNs and associations without touching the target, SOC analysts check whether a host is 'ours' during incidents, DNS administrators audit what their zones and CT logs reveal, and Go developers drive its engine API or build on OAM. Alternatives include subfinder, assetfinder, findomain, puredns/shuffledns with massdns, BBOT, SpiderFoot and Recon-ng, plus commercial ASM platforms such as Microsoft Defender EASM and Cortex Xpanse.
